Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun for best color and flowering. Well-draining soil. Fertilize in spring. Prune in late winter—cut hard for large leaves, light prune for plumes. Purple cultivars need full sun. Drought tolerant. Fall color orange to red. Mildly toxic to pets—sap may cause irritation; ingestion may cause GI upset.

Water regularly when young; established trees need supplemental water only during drought. Full sun preferred; tolerates light shade. Acidic, well-drained, moist soil. Fertilize in early spring with acidic evergreen fertilizer. Prune only dead or damaged branches — do not cut into old wood as it won't regrow. Shallow root system — susceptible to wind throw. Blue spruce is one of the most popular landscape conifers. Prone to spider mites in hot, dry conditions. Non-toxic to pets.

Keep soil moist when young. Full sun preferred. Tolerates wet or dry soil. Fertilize in spring when establishing. Prune in late winter. Fall color red, orange, yellow. Seed balls can be messy—consider fruitless cultivars. Deep taproot.

Water regularly during establishment; very tolerant of drought and urban conditions once mature. Full sun preferred. Highly adaptable to most soil types and pH levels. Fertilize annually in spring. Prune in winter to maintain clearance and shape. London plane is the premier urban tree — tolerates pollution, compacted soil, heat, and heavy pruning. Distinctive bark is ornamental year-round. Produces spiky seed balls. Very large tree (30m+) — needs ample space. Non-toxic to pets.

Water deeply and regularly during establishment and dry spells; somewhat drought-sensitive. Full sun preferred. Prefers deep, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil. Fertilize young trees in early spring. Fast-growing shade tree. Prune in late winter when dormant. Aphids on leaves may produce sticky honeydew. Brilliant golden-yellow fall color. Non-toxic to pets.

Thrives in moist to wet soil; ideal near ponds, streams, and low-lying areas. Full sun preferred. Extremely fast-growing — can add 2-3m per year. Plant well away from foundations, septic systems, and underground pipes as roots are aggressive. Prune dead or damaged branches in late winter. Short-lived for a tree (30-50 years). Very cold-hardy. Non-toxic to pets.

Keep soil consistently moist; thrives near water. Full sun. Plant away from pipes and foundations—aggressive roots. Prune in late winter. Fast growth. Short-lived (30–50 years). Weak wood—susceptible to storm damage. Avoid in small yards.

Water regularly; prefers consistently moist but not waterlogged soil. Partial shade to full sun. Prefers acidic, well-draining soil. Surprisingly adaptable in cultivation. Hardy to about -5°C. Slow growing. Non-toxic. Conservation status: critically endangered in the wild. Prune dead, diseased, or crossing branches. Best done during dormancy. Maintain central leader or natural form.

Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun to partial shade. Well-draining soil. Fertilize in spring. Prune lightly after flowering. Semi-evergreen to evergreen. Attracts pollinators. Deer resistant.

Full sun to partial shade — at least 6 hours of sun for dense foliage. Water deeply once per week when young; established trees tolerate moderate drought. Well-drained soil essential — does not tolerate waterlogged conditions. Tolerates wide pH (6.0-8.0). Prune lightly in spring to shape. Protect from heavy snow and ice damage. Keep soil consistently moist but well-drained (2-3 times per week). Acidic soil essential (pH 4.5-6.0) - use acidifying fertilizer and mulch with pine needles or oak leaves. Deciduous varieties: reduce watering when dormant in winter. Toxic to pets.

Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun for best color. Tolerates poor soil. Fertilize in spring. Prune in late winter—wear gloves for thorns. Deer resistant. Invasive in eastern North America—check local restrictions. Consider sterile cultivars. Mildly toxic to pets—may cause GI upset if ingested.

Water regularly during establishment; moderately drought-tolerant once mature. Full sun to partial shade—more sun means more berries. Adaptable to most well-drained soils. Fertilize lightly in spring. Can be cut back hard to the ground in late winter to rejuvenate (blooms on new wood). Berries attract birds. Non-toxic to pets.

Water regularly during establishment; very drought tolerant once mature. Full sun essential for best flowering. Highly adaptable to poor, sandy, or clay soils; tolerates some salinity. Minimal fertilization needed — native plant adapted to nutrient-poor Australian soils. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain shape — do not cut into old wood. Excellent for coastal gardens. Seed capsules persist on branches for years. Attracts hummingbirds, bees, and honeyeaters. Non-toxic to pets.

Keep soil evenly moist, especially during establishment. Well-drained soil essential. Full sun to partial shade. Fertilize in early spring with balanced fertilizer. Evergreen; reduce watering in winter when growth slows. Toxic to pets.

Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun for best fall color. Adapts to most soils. Fertilize in spring. Prune in late winter. Invasive in eastern North America—avoid or use sterile cultivars. Berries toxic. Corky "wings" on stems distinctive. Toxic to pets.

Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun essential. Well-draining soil. Fertilize in spring. Prune hard in late winter—flowers on new growth. Deadhead to prolong bloom. Invasive in some regions—choose sterile cultivars. Deer resistant.

Keep soil evenly moist (weekly deep watering). Well-drained, acidic soil essential. Partial shade preferred - avoid hot afternoon sun. Fertilize in spring with acid-loving plant fertilizer. Evergreen; reduce watering in winter when growth slows.

Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun preferred. Well-draining soil. Fertilize in spring. Cut back hard in late winter—flowers on new growth. Drought tolerant. Attracts bees and butterflies. Deer resistant. Late-season bloomer.

Deep soak regularly during growing season. Water well before ground freezes in winter to prevent winter desiccation (brown needles). Mulch around base to retain moisture and protect roots. Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun to partial shade. Well-draining soil. Fertilize in spring. Prune after berries drop. Fire blight susceptible. Berries attract birds. Some species invasive—check locally. Drought tolerant once established. Toxic to pets.

Water moderately — keep evenly moist but never waterlogged; daphnes are very sensitive to root rot. Partial shade preferred; protect from hot afternoon sun. Water regularly during establishment; drought tolerant once mature. Full sun to partial shade — evergreen varieties tolerate shade well. Highly adaptable to most soils. Fertilize once in spring. Deep soak regularly (weekly during growing season). Keep consistently moist during establishment (first 1-2 years). Water well before ground freezes in winter to prevent desiccation. Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun for best color. Well-draining, slightly acidic soil. Fertilize in spring. Prune after flowering. Purple cultivars need sun for color. Cold-sensitive in marginal zones. Fast-growing. Versatile size.

Susceptible to leaf spot (Entomosporium) in humid climates — ensure good air circulation. Fast-growing. Mildly toxic to pets (contains cyanogenic glycosides in seeds).

Keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged; water deeply during dry periods. Partial shade preferred—morning sun with afternoon shade is ideal. Water regularly during bloom season; drought-tolerant once established. Full sun produces heaviest flowering; tolerates partial shade. Prune hard in late winter to encourage bushy growth. Water regularly during establishment; moderately drought tolerant once mature. Full sun to partial shade. Highly adaptable to most soil types and pH levels. Fertilize once in spring. Water regularly during establishment; drought tolerant once mature. Full sun for best berry production; tolerates partial shade. Adaptable to most well-drained soils. Fertilize once in spring. Berries persist through winter, providing vital food for birds. Can be trained as espalier on walls and fences. Berries are mildly toxic raw but can be cooked into jelly. Mildly toxic to pets.

Keep soil consistently moist but well-drained (2-3 times per week). Acidic soil essential (pH 4.5-6.0) - use acidifying fertilizer and mulch with pine needles or oak leaves. Excellent for Mediterranean gardens. Evergreen; reduce watering in winter when growth slows.

Regular deep watering at base (2-3 times per week during growing season). Avoid wetting leaves to prevent disease (black spot, powdery mildew). Mulch around base to retain moisture. Full sun essential (6-8 hours daily). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with rose fertilizer. Prune in late winter/early spring. Deadhead spent flowers to encourage reblooming. Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun essential. Well-draining soil; drought tolerant. Fertilize sparingly. Cut back to ground in late winter. Deer resistant. Attracts pollinators.

Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun preferred. Adapts to most soils. Fertilize in spring. Spring bloomers: prune after flowering. Summer bloomers: prune in late winter. Tough and easy. Many cultivars for size and color.

Water regularly but do not overwater — root rot is the main killer. Morning sun with afternoon shade is ideal; protect blooms from hot afternoon sun. Keep soil evenly moist, especially during flowering and fruiting. Well-drained soil preferred. Full sun to partial shade. Fertilize in early spring with balanced fertilizer. Provide support for climbing habit. Self-fertile but cross-pollination improves yield. Harvest when fully colored and slightly soft. Require warm climates. Popular tropical fruit. Evergreen; reduce watering in winter when growth slows. Remove dead or rotting sections promptly.

Water regularly and deeply; needs consistent moisture during flowering and fruiting. Full sun essential for fruit production. Very high humidity (80%+) required—strictly tropical. Deep, well-draining, acidic clay-loam soil (pH 5.0-6.5). Fertilize regularly with balanced fertilizer; increase potassium during fruiting. Extremely tall tree (25-40 meters)—not practical for containers. Fruit takes 3-5 months to ripen after pollination. Pollinated by bats at night. First fruit after 5-7 years from seed. Non-toxic to pets. Prune during dormancy. Remove dead and diseased wood. Thin to improve fruit size and air circulation.

Keep soil evenly moist (weekly deep watering). Well-drained soil preferred. Full sun to partial shade. Fertilize in early spring with balanced fertilizer. Prune in late winter to remove old canes. Most varieties need cross-pollination - plant 2+ varieties. Harvest clusters when fully ripe (dark purple/black). Berries must be cooked before eating. Toxic to pets - raw berries, leaves, stems contain cyanogenic glycosides. Popular for health benefits and jellies. Deciduous varieties: reduce watering when dormant in winter.

Deep soak weekly during growing season. Consistent moisture important during fruit development. Mulch around base. Full sun essential (6-8 hours daily). Fertilize in early spring with balanced fertilizer. Prune in late winter. Self-fertile. Some varieties produce two crops (breba and main crop). Can be grown in containers. Harvest when soft and drooping. Protect from cold in winter if needed. Deciduous; reduce or withhold watering when leaves drop in fall.

Water deeply but infrequently once established (every 1-2 weeks). Very drought tolerant. Well-drained soil preferred. Full sun essential. Fertilize in spring with balanced fertilizer. Prune in late winter to maintain shape. Self-fertile. Harvest berries when fully red. Popular superfood. Can be grown in containers. Very popular in China. Deciduous varieties: reduce watering when dormant in winter.

Water consistently to keep soil evenly moist, about 1 inch per week - drought stress causes premature fruit drop. Partial shade to full sun; tolerates more shade than most fruit bushes, and benefits from afternoon shade in warmer zones. Fertilize lightly in early spring with balanced fertilizer. Prune in late winter to maintain an open, goblet-shaped form for air circulation - this reduces mildew, which gooseberries are prone to. Wear thick gloves when harvesting due to sharp thorns. Mulch to keep roots cool in summer. Non-toxic to pets.

Water deeply every 7-10 days; consistent moisture during fruit development. Full sun essential — needs more heat than other citrus for sweetest fruit. Well-drained, acidic soil. Fertilize 3-4 times per year with citrus fertilizer. Prune to remove dead wood and maintain airflow. Fruits can remain on the tree for months after ripening. Interacts with many medications (furanocoumarins inhibit drug metabolism). Mildly toxic to pets.

Deep watering weekly during growing season. Consistent moisture important during fruit development. Mulch around base. Full sun essential (6-8 hours daily). Fertilize in early spring with balanced fertilizer. Prune heavily in late winter - grapes fruit on new growth from previous year's wood. Provide strong support (trellis, arbor). Harvest when fully ripe and sweet. Many varieties need winter chill. Research specific variety for exact pruning requirements. Deciduous varieties: reduce watering when dormant in winter.

Water regularly to keep soil moist but not waterlogged during the growing season; reduce watering in winter. Full sun essential for best fruit production (6-8 hours daily). Fertilize every 1-2 months during the growing season with a balanced fertilizer - guavas are moderate feeders. Prune lightly to shape and to improve air circulation, which reduces disease. Guavas are remarkably adaptable and can fruit within 2-3 years from seed. Protect from frost; mature trees tolerate brief dips to -2°C but young trees are more tender. Non-toxic to pets.

Water regularly during growing season; keep soil evenly moist but never waterlogged. Full sun essential for fruit production. High humidity (60%+) preferred. Deep, well-draining, fertile soil. Fertilize quarterly with balanced fertilizer, increasing potassium during fruiting. Young trees are frost-sensitive—protect below 10°C. Fruits grow directly from the trunk (cauliflory). Can grow 15-20 meters tall; choose dwarf cultivars for containers. Latex sap is sticky—oil hands before handling fruit. Non-toxic to pets. Deep soak weekly during growing season. Drought tolerant once established. Well-drained soil preferred. Full sun essential. Fertilize in early spring with balanced fertilizer. Prune to maintain shape. Self-fertile but better with cross-pollination. Harvest when fully red and slightly wrinkled. Can be eaten fresh or dried. Very popular in China. Drought tolerant. Deciduous; reduce or withhold watering when leaves drop in fall.

Water regularly to keep soil consistently moist but well-drained; kiwis have shallow roots and are sensitive to drought. Full sun to partial shade, with protection from strong winds. Fertilize in spring with a balanced fertilizer - avoid over-fertilizing which promotes leaf growth over fruit. Both male and female vines are required for pollination (one male can pollinate up to 8 females). Provide a sturdy trellis or pergola, as mature vines become extremely heavy. Prune vigorously in winter and lightly in summer to control rampant growth. Non-toxic to pets.

Keep soil evenly moist during growing season. Well-drained soil essential. Full sun essential. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with citrus fertilizer. Prune to maintain size. Self-fertile. Harvest when fully orange. Entire fruit is edible including peel. Cold-hardier than most citrus - can tolerate light frosts. Can be grown in containers. Evergreen; reduce watering in winter when growth slows.

Water deeply when top 2 inches of soil are dry; do not let roots sit in water. Full sun essential (8+ hours for best fruiting). Acidic, well-drained soil (pH 5.5-6.5). Fertilize monthly spring through fall with citrus-specific fertilizer high in nitrogen. Prune to shape and remove suckers below the graft. Protect from frost — Meyer lemon tolerates brief dips to -3°C; Eureka is more cold-sensitive. Yellow leaves often indicate iron deficiency (use chelated iron). Excellent container plant; dwarf varieties fruit well in pots. Mildly toxic to pets (essential oils and psoralen in peel).

Water regularly to keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged. Full sun essential (6-8 hours). Acidic, well-drained soil. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with citrus fertilizer. More cold-sensitive than other citrus — protect below 10°C. Key limes are smaller, more aromatic, and seedier; Persian limes are the standard grocery variety (seedless). Excellent container plant — dwarf varieties thrive in pots and can be brought indoors in winter. Mildly toxic to pets. Prune during dormancy. Remove dead and diseased wood. Thin to improve fruit size and air circulation.

Keep soil evenly moist during growing season. Well-drained, slightly acidic soil preferred. Full sun essential. Fertilize in spring and summer with balanced fertilizer. Prune to maintain size. Self-fertile. Harvest when skin is brown and fruit is sweet. Require tropical or subtropical climate. Related to lychee. Popular in Chinese cuisine. Evergreen; reduce watering in winter when growth slows.

Deep soak weekly during growing season. Well-drained soil preferred. Full sun to partial shade. Fertilize in spring and summer with balanced fertilizer. Prune to maintain size and shape. Self-fertile. Harvest when fully yellow-orange and slightly soft. Can tolerate some cold but protect from hard freezes. Popular in China and Japan. Evergreen; reduce watering in winter when growth slows.

Keep soil evenly moist during growing season. Well-drained, acidic soil preferred. Full sun essential. Fertilize in spring and summer with citrus fertilizer. Prune to maintain size. Self-fertile but cross-pollination improves yield. Harvest when skin is pink-red and fruit is fragrant. Require tropical or subtropical climate - protect from frost. Very popular in China. Evergreen; reduce watering in winter when growth slows.

Water deeply when top 2 inches of soil are dry; reduce in winter. Full sun essential. Acidic, well-drained soil. Fertilize 3-4 times per year with citrus fertilizer. The most cold-hardy citrus group — satsumas tolerate brief dips to -8°C. Easy-to-peel fruits are among the sweetest citrus. Many varieties are seedless. Excellent for containers. Harvest when fruit is fully colored and slightly soft. Mildly toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Water deeply once or twice per week during the growing season, then reduce significantly during winter dormancy - mangoes prefer a distinct dry period to stimulate flowering. Full sun essential (8+ hours daily). Fertilize 3-4 times per year with a citrus or fruit tree fertilizer. Caution: mango sap and skin contain urushiol (the same compound as poison ivy) and can cause contact dermatitis - wear gloves when pruning. Prune after harvest to maintain manageable size. Protect from frost; tropical tree that needs consistently warm temperatures. Mildly toxic to pets; sap and skin can cause irritation.

Water regularly during the first two years to establish; mature trees are quite drought tolerant. Full sun to partial shade (6+ hours daily). Fertilize once in late winter with a balanced fertilizer - mulberries are not heavy feeders and over-fertilizing reduces fruit quality. Prune in winter to shape and remove crossing branches. Mulberries fruit prolifically and fruit stains everything it touches - avoid planting near walkways, driveways, or patios. Fast-growing trees that can reach 30-50 feet; consider dwarf cultivars for smaller spaces. Non-toxic to pets; unripe fruit and raw leaves may cause mild stomach upset.
Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun preferred for most. Fertilize regularly during growing season. Harvest as needed. Mulch to retain moisture. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Deep soak weekly during growing season. Increase watering during fruit development. Mulch around base. Full sun essential (6-8 hours daily). Fertilize in early spring with fruit tree fertilizer. Prune in late winter/early spring. Most varieties are self-fertile. Smooth skin unlike peaches. Thin fruit for larger nectarines. Protect from late frosts during flowering. Harvest when fully colored. Requires winter chill. Reduce watering when dormant in winter.

Water deeply but infrequently once established - olives are very drought tolerant and overwatering is the most common mistake. Full sun essential (8+ hours daily). Fertilize lightly in spring with a balanced or nitrogen-focused fertilizer. Thrives in poor, rocky, well-draining soil; heavy clay causes root rot. Prune annually in late winter to maintain an open center and promote air circulation. Requires winter chill hours (200-700 depending on variety) and warm, dry summers for fruit set. Extremely long-lived - can produce for centuries. Non-toxic to pets.

Water deeply when top 2 inches of soil are dry; consistent moisture important during fruit development. Full sun essential (6-8 hours). Acidic, well-drained soil preferred. Fertilize 3-4 times per year with citrus fertilizer. Prune sparingly — mainly remove dead wood and suckers. Protect from hard frost; mature trees tolerate brief dips to -3°C. Navel oranges are best eaten fresh; Valencia is preferred for juice. Trees can fruit and flower simultaneously. Mildly toxic to pets.

Water regularly to keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged - papayas have fleshy trunks that rot easily in soggy conditions. Full sun essential (6-8 hours daily). Feed heavily every 2 weeks with balanced fertilizer, as papayas are extremely fast growers that fruit within 6-12 months from seed. Excellent drainage is critical; plant on a mound if soil is heavy. Protect from wind, which can topple the shallow-rooted trunk. Cannot tolerate any frost - even brief exposure below 0°C is fatal. Toxic to pets; latex in unripe fruit and leaves is harmful. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Water regularly to keep soil evenly moist during the growing season; reduce in winter. Full sun essential for maximum flowering and fruit set (6-8 hours daily). Fertilize every 4-6 weeks during the growing season with a fertilizer low in nitrogen but high in potassium and phosphorus to promote fruiting over vine growth. Provide a strong trellis or fence for climbing, as vines grow vigorously up to 20 feet per season. Most varieties need cross-pollination from a different cultivar for reliable fruit set. Fruits are ripe when they fall from the vine or the skin wrinkles. Non-toxic to pets; unripe fruit contains trace cyanide compounds. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Water regularly to keep soil consistently moist - pawpaws are understory trees naturally found along stream banks and do not tolerate drought well. Partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun for fruiting as the tree matures. Fertilize in spring with a balanced organic fertilizer; avoid high-nitrogen synthetic fertilizers. Needs a different genetic individual (not just a different branch) for cross-pollination; plant at least two unrelated seedlings. Flowers are pollinated by flies and beetles, not bees - some growers hang rotting meat near blooms to attract pollinators. Fruit bruises easily and has a very short shelf life of 2-5 days. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead, rotten, diseased leaves and the parts that may affect the good appearance

Deep soak weekly during growing season. Increase watering during fruit development. Mulch around base. Full sun essential (6-8 hours daily). Fertilize in early spring with fruit tree fertilizer. Prune in late winter/early spring. Most varieties are self-fertile. Thin fruit for larger peaches. Protect from late frosts during flowering. Harvest when easily twists off branch. Requires winter chill. Reduce watering when dormant in winter.

Deep soak weekly during growing season. Increase watering during fruit development. Mulch around base. Full sun essential (6-8 hours daily). Fertilize in early spring with fruit tree fertilizer. Prune in late winter/early spring. Most varieties need cross-pollination - plant compatible varieties. Harvest when mature but still firm - ripen off tree. Requires winter chill. Research specific type (European vs Asian) for exact requirements. Reduce watering when dormant in winter.

Deep soak weekly during growing season. Well-drained soil preferred. Full sun essential. Fertilize in early spring with balanced fertilizer. Prune to maintain shape. Most varieties are self-fertile. Harvest astringent varieties when very soft; non-astringent when firm. Popular in both USA and China. Requires winter chill for best fruiting. Deciduous; reduce or withhold watering when leaves drop in fall.

Water sparingly, allowing soil to dry between waterings - as a bromeliad, pineapple stores water in its leaf rosette and is prone to root rot in soggy soil. Full sun essential (6-8 hours daily) for fruit production. Fertilize monthly during the growing season with a balanced liquid fertilizer, including foliar feeding by spraying into the rosette. Plant from the crown of a store-bought pineapple by twisting it off, letting the base dry for a few days, then planting in well-draining soil. Each plant produces only one fruit over 18-24 months, then produces offsets (ratoons) that will fruit again. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Full sun — 6-8 hours direct sunlight daily. Keep soil consistently moist; never let it dry out completely. Thrives at 25-30°C; cannot tolerate below 10°C. Rich, well-drained soil with high organic matter (pH 6.0-7.5). Heavy feeder — fertilize monthly with balanced fertilizer. Mulch thickly to retain moisture. Protect from wind which shreds leaves. Each stem fruits once then dies — new suckers continue the cycle. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Deep soak weekly during growing season. Increase watering during fruit development. Mulch around base. Full sun essential (6-8 hours daily). Fertilize in early spring with fruit tree fertilizer. Prune in late winter/early spring. Many varieties need cross-pollination - plant compatible varieties. Thin fruit for larger plums. Harvest when fully colored and slightly soft. Requires winter chill. Reduce watering when dormant in winter.

Deep soak weekly during growing season. Drought tolerant once established. Mulch around base. Full sun essential (6-8 hours daily). Fertilize in early spring with balanced fertilizer. Prune to maintain shape. Self-fertile. Harvest when fully colored and makes metallic sound when tapped. Can be grown in containers. Requires hot summers for best fruiting. Deciduous; reduce or withhold watering when leaves drop in fall.

Deep soak regularly during growing season. Well-drained soil essential. Full sun essential. Fertilize monthly spring through fall with citrus fertilizer. Prune to maintain size. Self-fertile. Harvest when fully yellow and fragrant. Largest citrus fruit. Require warm climates - protect from frost. Popular in China and Southeast Asia. Evergreen; reduce watering in winter when growth slows.

Water very sparingly - soak soil thoroughly then allow to dry completely before watering again; in winter, suspend watering almost entirely. Full sun essential (8+ hours daily). Fertilize once in spring with a dilute cactus fertilizer or low-nitrogen blend. Do NOT mulch - prickly pear needs bare, fast-draining soil and mulch retains too much moisture causing rot. Use tongs and thick gloves when harvesting fruit (tunas), as both fruit and pads have glochids (tiny barbed spines). Extremely drought and heat tolerant once established. Pads can be rooted simply by setting a cut pad on dry soil. Non-toxic to pets; glochids can cause mechanical irritation. Remove dead or rotting sections promptly.

Water regularly during the first few years to establish; mature trees are moderately drought tolerant. Full sun essential for best fruit production (6-8 hours daily). Fertilize in early spring with a balanced fruit tree fertilizer. Prune in late winter to maintain an open, vase-shaped canopy - quince fruits on the tips of new growth, so avoid heavy heading cuts. Fruit is too hard and astringent to eat raw but becomes beautifully fragrant and turns rosy-pink when cooked into preserves, membrillo paste, or poached. Very ornamental with large pink-white spring blossoms. Susceptible to fire blight - prune affected branches 12 inches below infection. Non-toxic to pets.

Water regularly; keep soil consistently moist, especially during flowering and fruiting. Full sun for best fruit production. Very high humidity (80%+) essential—strictly tropical, no frost tolerance. Deep, well-draining, organically rich acidic soil (pH 5.0-6.5). Fertilize quarterly with balanced fertilizer; increase potassium during fruiting. Trees are either male or female—plant both for pollination or choose grafted hermaphrodite varieties. Can grow 15-25 meters; choose grafted dwarf cultivars for smaller spaces. Non-toxic to pets. Prune during dormancy. Remove dead and diseased wood. Thin to improve fruit size and air circulation.

Keep soil evenly moist (weekly deep watering). Water at base to avoid wetting fruit. Mulch around plants to retain moisture and suppress weeds. Full sun essential (6-8 hours daily). Fertilize in early spring with balanced fertilizer. Prune according to type - summer-bearing: remove fruited canes after harvest; everbearing: can be pruned for one or two crops. Support canes with trellis. Harvest when fully colored and easily detaches. Replace plants every 8-10 years. Deciduous varieties: reduce watering when dormant in winter.

Full sun — minimum 6-7 hours direct sunlight daily for fruiting. Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged; water deeply 2-3 times per week. Thrives at 20-35°C; young trees killed by frost, mature trees survive brief dips to -3°C. Acidic, well-drained soil (pH 5.5-6.5). Fertilize monthly during growing season. Contains high oxalic acid — toxic to those with kidney disease and mildly toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Keep soil evenly moist (2-3 times per week). Water at base to avoid wetting fruit which can cause rot. Mulch with straw or pine needles to keep berries clean and prevent soil contact. Full sun essential (6-8 hours daily). Fertilize in early spring and after harvest with balanced fertilizer. Remove runners first year to encourage fruiting; allow runners second year to propagate. Harvest when fully red. Replace plants every 3-4 years. Research variety type (June-bearing, everbearing, day-neutral) for exact requirements. Seasonal crop; watering varies by growing zone and harvest timing. Prune during dormancy. Remove dead and diseased wood. Thin to improve fruit size and air circulation.

Full sun essential — cannot grow in shade. Water regularly when young to establish deep roots; mature trees are drought-tolerant. Let soil dry between waterings. Well-drained soil; tolerates sandy, loamy, or slightly acidic conditions (pH 6.0-7.5). Thrives at 25-40°C; frost-sensitive. Slow to fruit — typically 6-8 years from seed. Fertilize annually in spring. Non-toxic to pets and humans. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Water deeply and consistently, providing 1-2 inches per week - critical during fruit development to prevent cracking and hollow heart. Full sun essential (8+ hours daily); needs long, hot growing season. Fertilize at planting with balanced fertilizer, then switch to a low-nitrogen, high-potassium formula when vines begin to flower. Give vines plenty of room to sprawl (6-10 feet in each direction) or train on a strong trellis with sling support for fruit. Ripe when the tendril nearest the fruit turns brown and dry, and the ground spot turns creamy yellow. Mulch heavily with straw to suppress weeds and keep fruit off wet soil. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Water deeply every 1-2 weeks during growing season; reduce in winter but do not let soil go completely dry. Full sun essential. Well-drained, sandy loam preferred — cannot tolerate waterlogged soil. Fertilize in early spring with nitrogen-rich fertilizer. Prune after harvest to maintain shape and improve air circulation. Needs 300-600 chill hours. Most varieties need a cross-pollinator. Blooms early — late frosts can destroy the crop. Bitter almond contains amygdalin (toxic); sweet almond is safe to eat. Mildly toxic to pets.

Water regularly during establishment; mature trees tolerate dry periods. Full sun essential. Sandy, well-drained soil preferred. Fertilize 2-3 times per year with balanced fertilizer. Prune to maintain manageable height and remove dead wood. The shell contains caustic oil (urushiol, same as poison ivy) — never eat raw cashew shells. The cashew apple (pseudofruit) is edible and used for juice. Frost-sensitive — tropical climates only. Mildly toxic to pets (shell oil is irritating).

Water regularly during first few years; established trees are moderately drought tolerant. Full sun essential for nut production. Acidic, well-drained, sandy loam preferred — cannot tolerate alkaline or waterlogged soil. Fertilize lightly in spring. Prune in late winter. Needs a cross-pollinator from a different variety. American chestnut was nearly wiped out by chestnut blight — Chinese chestnut is blight-resistant. Nuts are starchy (unlike most tree nuts) and can be roasted, boiled, or ground into flour. Non-toxic to pets.

Water regularly during establishment and nut development; mature plants are moderately drought tolerant. Full sun to partial shade. Adaptable to most well-drained soils. Fertilize once in early spring with balanced fertilizer. Prune suckers regularly to maintain tree form, or allow to grow as multi-stemmed shrub. Wind-pollinated — plant at least two different cultivars for cross-pollination. Harvest when husks turn brown and nuts fall naturally. Non-toxic to pets.

Water regularly — macadamias need consistent moisture, especially during nut development. Full sun for best production. Acidic, well-drained soil essential — does not tolerate alkaline conditions. Fertilize 3-4 times per year with citrus or avocado fertilizer. Protect from strong winds (shallow root system). Trees take 7-10 years to reach full production. Wind-pollinated but benefits from bee activity. Highly toxic to dogs — even one or two nuts can cause weakness, tremors, and hyperthermia. Toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Water deeply and regularly, especially during nut filling (July-September) — pecans are heavy water users. Full sun essential. Deep, well-drained alluvial soil preferred. Fertilize with zinc-containing fertilizer in spring — zinc deficiency is common. Prune young trees to develop a central leader. Most varieties need a cross-pollinator (Type I × Type II). Trees can take 6-10 years to bear. Alternate bearing is common. Non-toxic to pets.

Water deeply but infrequently — pistachios are very drought tolerant once established. Full sun essential; needs hot summers. Well-drained, even alkaline soil tolerated — one of few nut trees that thrives in poor, calcareous soil. Fertilize sparingly. Dioecious — plant one male per 8-10 female trees. Trees take 5-8 years to bear. Needs both hot summers and cold winters (600+ chill hours). Alternate bearing (heavy one year, light the next). Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Water deeply once a week during growing season; established trees are drought tolerant. Full sun essential (6-8 hours). Well-drained, deep soil preferred — shallow or compacted soil stunts growth. Fertilize annually in early spring with balanced fertilizer. Prune in late winter when dormant to shape and remove dead wood. Black walnuts produce juglone, which is toxic to many plants — avoid planting tomatoes, apples, or azaleas within the drip line. Harvest when hulls begin to split in autumn. Trees need 400-1500 chill hours depending on variety. Mildly toxic to pets (hulls can cause GI upset).

Full sun essential — minimum 6-8 hours direct sunlight. Very drought-tolerant; water only when soil is completely dry. Sandy, well-draining soil with alkaline pH (7.5-8.0). Thrives at 25-35°C; frost-sensitive below -1°C. Annual in cold climates, perennial in zones 8+. Minimal fertilizer needed. Harvest roots after first year of growth. Berries are mildly toxic — keep away from children and pets. Harvest regularly to promote bushy growth. Pinch off flower buds to extend leaf production.

Keep soil evenly moist (2-3 times per week). Water at base to avoid wetting leaves. Well-drained soil essential. Full sun preferred (6-8 hours daily). Fertilize every 3-4 weeks with balanced fertilizer. Pinch flowers immediately to prolong leaf production. Harvest regularly by pinching tips to encourage bushy growth. Very sensitive to cold - plant after last frost. Annual - replant each season.

Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun preferred. Fertilize regularly during growing season. Harvest leaves as needed; dry before storing. Mulch to retain moisture. Mildly toxic to pets if ingested. Cut useless and excessively grown top branches, keep the height of the whole plant at about 3.5m

Water moderately, allowing soil to dry slightly between waterings - borage is fairly drought tolerant once established. Full sun to partial shade (6+ hours daily). Fertilizing is generally unnecessary; borage thrives in poor to average soil and excess nitrogen produces leggy growth with fewer flowers. Sow seeds directly outdoors as borage has a long taproot and resents transplanting. Self-seeds prolifically - deadhead to control spread, or allow it to naturalize. Harvest young leaves (older leaves become prickly) and blue star-shaped flowers for salads and garnishes. Non-toxic to pets; flowers and young leaves are edible.
Keep soil consistently moist. High humidity. Partial shade. Warm temperatures. Harvest seed pods when green and before splitting. Tropical perennial. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Water moderately, allowing soil to dry between waterings - catnip is drought tolerant and prefers not to sit in wet soil. Full sun to partial shade (4-6 hours daily). Fertilize sparingly or not at all; rich soil and heavy feeding reduce the essential oil concentration that gives catnip its potency. Cut back by one-third after the first flush of flowers to encourage a second bloom. Be aware that cats will roll in, chew, and crush the plants - consider a protective cage if growing for harvest. Spreads by both runners and self-seeding; contain in pots or harvest frequently to control. Non-toxic to pets; the nepetalactone compound is safe and acts as a stimulant for cats.

Water regularly but lightly, keeping soil slightly moist - chamomile has shallow roots but does not like soggy soil. Full sun to partial shade (4-6 hours daily). Fertilizing is generally unnecessary and can reduce flower production and essential oil concentration. Sow seeds on the soil surface (they need light to germinate) in spring or fall. Harvest flower heads when petals begin to fold back from the center, typically in the morning after dew has dried. German chamomile is annual and self-seeds freely; Roman chamomile is a low-growing perennial useful as a fragrant ground cover. Non-toxic to pets; may cause reactions in those with ragweed allergies. After flowering remove the withered flowers, the part on the ground will wither in winter, the plant germinates again in spring

Water regularly to keep soil consistently moist - chervil bolts quickly if stressed by drought. Partial shade is essential, NOT full sun; chervil is one of the few herbs that actually prefers and needs shade, especially in warm climates. Fertilize lightly once a month with a balanced liquid fertilizer. Sow seeds directly outdoors in early spring or late summer/fall, as chervil dislikes transplanting and heat. Best treated as a cool-season crop; it bolts rapidly in temperatures above 24°C. Harvest outer leaves regularly, cutting stems at the base. Flavor is delicate and lost when cooked - add fresh at the end. Non-toxic to pets. Harvest regularly to promote bushy growth. Pinch off flower buds to extend leaf production.

Keep soil evenly moist (2-3 times per week). Well-drained soil preferred. Full sun to partial shade. Fertilize monthly with balanced fertilizer. Harvest by cutting leaves at base. Divide every 3-4 years. Perennial - returns each year. Garlic flavor. Essential in Chinese cuisine. Can be grown in containers. Edible white flowers. Herbaceous perennials die back; reduce watering when dormant. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Keep soil evenly moist (2-3 times per week). Well-drained soil preferred. Full sun to partial shade. Fertilize monthly with balanced fertilizer. Harvest by cutting leaves at base. Divide every 3-4 years. Perennial - returns each year. Easy to grow. Can be grown in containers. Edible purple flowers. Reduce watering in winter when growth slows. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Keep soil evenly moist (2-3 times per week). Consistent moisture prevents bolting. Well-drained soil preferred. Full sun to partial shade. Prefer cooler temperatures - plant in spring or fall. Fertilize every 3-4 weeks with balanced fertilizer. Harvest leaves regularly. Bolts quickly in heat - provide shade in summer or plant in fall. Annual - replant each season. Seeds (coriander) can be harvested when brown. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Water when top inch of soil is dry. Full sun preferred. Fertilize regularly. Use as compost activator or mulch. Do not consume internally. Mildly toxic to pets when ingested. Harvest regularly to promote bushy growth. Pinch off flower buds to extend leaf production.

Water moderately — keep soil evenly moist during germination and early growth, then reduce. Overwatering causes root rot. Full sun essential; needs long, hot growing season (3-4 months frost-free). Well-drained, sandy loam soil. Direct sow after last frost — does not transplant well. Seeds mature when plants turn brown; harvest entire plant and dry upside down. Flavor is much stronger when seeds are toasted before use. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Keep soil evenly moist (2-3 times per week). Well-drained soil preferred. Full sun essential. Fertilize every 3-4 weeks with balanced fertilizer. Harvest leaves regularly. Harvest seeds when brown. Can bolt in heat - plant in spring or fall. Both leaves and seeds are used. Attracts beneficial insects. Annual - replant each season. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Water sparingly, allowing soil to dry between waterings - epazote is drought tolerant and actually produces more aromatic oils under slightly dry conditions. Full sun preferred (6-8 hours daily). Fertilizing is unnecessary; epazote thrives in poor, well-draining soil and excessive nutrients reduce flavor intensity. Self-seeds very aggressively and can become weedy - deadhead before seeds mature or grow in containers. Use leaves sparingly in cooking, as the flavor is very strong and the plant contains toxic compounds (ascaridole) that are harmful in large quantities. Harvest young leaves, which are milder than mature foliage. Toxic to pets in large quantities; contains ascaridole which is harmful if ingested in excess.

Keep soil evenly moist; water regularly in hot weather. Full sun essential—at least 6 hours daily. Medium humidity fine. Deep, well-draining, fertile soil. Fertilize at planting with compost; side-dress with balanced fertilizer mid-season. Do not plant near dill—they cross-pollinate and produce poor-flavored seeds. Hill soil around Florence fennel bulbs to blanch them. Attracts swallowtail butterfly caterpillars. Mildly toxic to pets in large amounts. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Keep soil evenly moist but not waterlogged. Well-drained, rich soil preferred. Partial shade preferred - avoid direct hot sun. Fertilize monthly with balanced fertilizer. Plant rhizome pieces with eyes pointing up. Harvest when leaves die back (8-10 months). Can be grown in containers. Essential spice in Chinese cuisine. Rhizomes can be harvested partially. Reduce watering in winter when growth slows. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Deep shade essential — 80% shade mimicking forest understory. Keep soil consistently moist but well-drained; never waterlogged. Prefers cool temperatures (18-21°C) and needs a winter cold period. Rich, loamy soil with high organic matter; pH 5.5-6.5. Extremely slow-growing — roots mature in 4-6 years. Do not fertilize. Susceptible to fungal diseases in humid conditions. Non-toxic to pets and humans. Harvest regularly to promote bushy growth. Pinch off flower buds to extend leaf production.

Water regularly to keep soil evenly moist but not waterlogged - holy basil likes consistent moisture but is more drought tolerant than sweet basil. Full sun essential (6-8 hours daily). Fertilize every 3-4 weeks with a balanced organic fertilizer; avoid heavy nitrogen which reduces the aromatic essential oil content. Pinch flower buds to prolong leaf harvest, though the purple flowers are also edible and attractive to pollinators. Unlike sweet basil, holy basil (tulsi) has a more clove-like, peppery flavor and is traditionally used in Thai stir-fries and Ayurvedic teas rather than Italian cuisine. Grows as a perennial in tropical zones but is treated as an annual in temperate climates. Non-toxic to pets.

Keep soil evenly moist but well-drained. Allow top inch to dry slightly between waterings. Avoid waterlogged soil - excellent drainage essential. Bright indirect to direct light (4-6 hours daily minimum). Medium humidity (40-50%) is fine. Fertilize monthly with balanced fertilizer at half strength. Harvest regularly to encourage bushy growth - pinch tips. Pinch flowers to prolong leaf production. Repot annually. Research specific herb for exact requirements.

Drought-tolerant once established; water deeply but infrequently, allowing soil to dry between waterings. Full sun essential—at least 6-8 hours daily. Low humidity preferred; good air circulation prevents fungal disease. Well-draining, slightly alkaline soil (add lime to acidic soils). Avoid rich fertilizer—lean soil concentrates fragrance. Prune after flowering by cutting back one-third; never cut into old wood. Mildly toxic to pets if ingested in large quantities.

Water regularly to keep soil evenly moist, but lemon balm is quite forgiving of occasional drought once established. Full sun to partial shade (4-6 hours daily); some afternoon shade in hot climates prevents leaf scorching. Fertilize sparingly - once or twice per season with compost or dilute balanced fertilizer is sufficient. Warning: lemon balm spreads extremely aggressively by both runners and self-seeding; grow in containers or use root barriers to prevent it from taking over the garden. Harvest frequently by cutting stems back to a leaf node, which keeps plants bushy and delays flowering. Cut the entire plant back by half in midsummer to rejuvenate growth. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead and pest-infested branches frequently

Keep soil evenly moist (2-3 times per week). Well-drained, rich soil preferred. Full sun preferred. Fertilize monthly with nitrogen-rich fertilizer. Harvest outer stalks at base. Divide every 2-3 years. Perennial in warm climates - treat as annual in cold. Can be grown in containers. Lemony flavor. Popular in Asian cuisine. Reduce watering in winter when growth slows. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Water regularly to keep soil consistently moist - lovage is a moisture-loving plant with deep roots. Full sun to partial shade (4-6 hours daily); appreciates afternoon shade in hot climates. Fertilize in early spring with compost or balanced fertilizer; lovage is a vigorous perennial that benefits from rich soil. Be prepared for its size - lovage grows 4-6 feet tall and should be placed at the back of the herb garden. Cut flower stalks before they bloom to direct energy into leaf production, unless saving seed. All parts are edible with an intense celery-like flavor: use leaves in soups and stews, hollow stems as savory straws, seeds as a spice, and roots as a cooked vegetable. Non-toxic to pets; may cause photosensitivity in some animals with heavy consumption. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Water moderately, allowing the top inch of soil to dry between waterings - marjoram prefers slightly drier conditions than most herbs and is susceptible to root rot in wet soil. Full sun essential (6-8 hours daily). Fertilize lightly every 4-6 weeks with a dilute liquid fertilizer; over-feeding diminishes the delicate sweet aroma. Harvest before flowers open for the strongest flavor by cutting stems back to a leaf pair. Tender perennial (hardy only to about -1°C); in cold climates grow as an annual or bring containers indoors for winter. Often confused with oregano but has a sweeter, milder, more floral flavor. Excellent for drying - hang bundles upside down in a warm, airy spot. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Keep soil evenly moist (2-3 times per week). Prefer consistently moist but well-drained soil. Full sun to partial shade. Fertilize monthly with balanced fertilizer. Harvest regularly to control growth. Very invasive - grow in containers or use barriers to contain. Spreads by runners. Can be grown indoors or outdoors. Perennial but may die back in winter. Reduce watering in winter when growth slows. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Water when soil is dry (every 1-2 weeks once established). Well-drained soil essential. Drought tolerant once established. Full sun preferred (6-8 hours daily). Fertilize sparingly in spring. Harvest regularly by cutting stems. Pinch flowers to prolong leaf production. Perennial - may need protection in very cold climates. Flavor intensifies when dried. Reduce watering in winter when growth slows.

Keep soil evenly moist (2-3 times per week). Well-drained soil preferred. Full sun to partial shade. Fertilize every 3-4 weeks with balanced fertilizer. Harvest outer leaves regularly to encourage new growth. Biennial but usually grown as annual. Flat-leaf has stronger flavor. Can be grown indoors. Very common culinary herb. Mildly toxic to pets in large amounts. Reduce watering in winter when growth slows. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Keep soil consistently moist; never let it dry out. Partial sun to partial shade—4-6 hours of sun ideal. Medium humidity fine. Rich, moisture-retentive soil. Fertilize monthly with balanced liquid fertilizer during growing season. Extremely invasive—always grow in containers to prevent spreading. Pinch tips regularly to promote bushy growth and prevent flowering. Harvest frequently; flavor is best just before flowering. Mildly toxic to pets (menthol can cause gastrointestinal upset).

Water when soil is dry (every 1-2 weeks once established). Well-drained soil essential. Drought tolerant once established. Full sun preferred. Fertilize sparingly in spring. Harvest leaves regularly. Prune to maintain shape. Perennial - may need protection in very cold climates. Strong flavor - use sparingly in cooking. Reduce watering in winter when growth slows.

Water moderately, allowing soil to dry slightly between waterings - savory prefers lean, well-drained conditions similar to other Mediterranean herbs. Full sun essential (6-8 hours daily). Fertilize sparingly or not at all; poor to average soil actually intensifies the peppery, thyme-like flavor. Summer savory (Satureja hortensis) is an annual with a milder flavor; winter savory (S. montana) is a hardy perennial with a stronger, more pungent taste. Harvest summer savory before flowering for best flavor; winter savory can be clipped year-round. Both types make excellent companion plants for beans and are traditionally used in bean dishes to aid digestion. Non-toxic to pets. Remove yellowing or damaged leaves promptly.

Water regularly to keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged. Full sun to partial shade (4-6 hours daily); some afternoon shade in hot climates prevents wilting and bitterness. Fertilize every 3-4 weeks with a balanced liquid fertilizer at half strength. Pinch growing tips regularly to encourage bushy growth and delay flowering. Available in green and red (purple) varieties - red shiso is used for coloring umeboshi and shiso juice, while green shiso is preferred fresh for sushi, sashimi, and rice wraps. Self-seeds freely and can become weedy if allowed to go to seed; deadhead or harvest before seed set. Direct sow after last frost as shiso resents transplanting. Non-toxic to pets.

Water regularly to keep soil evenly moist - sorrel's flavor becomes excessively sour and leaves turn tough in dry conditions. Full sun to partial shade (4-6 hours daily); benefits from afternoon shade in hot climates. Fertilize lightly in spring with compost or balanced fertilizer; too much nitrogen encourages excessive leaf growth with reduced flavor. Remove flower stalks promptly to prolong leaf harvest and prevent the plant from going to seed. A hardy perennial that returns reliably each spring and can be harvested for many years from the same clump. Leaves contain oxalic acid giving the signature tangy flavor - avoid consuming in very large quantities or if prone to kidney stones. Non-toxic to pets in small amounts; large quantities may cause issues due to oxalic acid. Remove dead and pest-infested branches frequently

Full sun for maximum flowering — tolerates partial shade. Drought-tolerant once established; water occasionally during dry spells. Adapts to most soil types including poor, sandy, or rocky soils. Well-drained soil preferred. Hardy to -20°C. Can become invasive — deadhead to prevent self-seeding. Contains hypericin which causes photosensitivity in livestock — toxic to horses and cattle. Mildly toxic to dogs and cats.

Water regularly to keep soil consistently moist but well-drained - stevia does not tolerate drought well, nor does it like sitting in water. Full sun to partial shade (6+ hours daily). Fertilize every 2-3 weeks during the growing season with a balanced fertilizer at half strength; avoid high-nitrogen formulas which dilute the sweet flavor. Pinch growing tips regularly to encourage bushy growth and more leaf production. Harvest leaves before flowering for maximum sweetness; once the plant blooms, leaves become less sweet and may turn bitter. Tender perennial hardy only to about 40°F (4°C); grow as an annual in cold climates or overwinter indoors. Leaves can be dried and ground into powder for a natural sweetener. Non-toxic to pets.

Water moderately, allowing soil to dry slightly between waterings - French tarragon prefers lean, well-drained conditions and will develop root rot in heavy, wet soil. Full sun to partial shade (6+ hours daily); tolerates light afternoon shade. Fertilize sparingly, once or twice per season with dilute balanced fertilizer; rich soil diminishes the distinctive anise flavor. French tarragon does NOT produce viable seed and must be propagated by root division or cuttings - if you see tarragon seeds for sale, they are Russian tarragon which has inferior flavor. Divide plants every 3-4 years in spring to maintain vigor. Harvest regularly to encourage new growth; flavor is strongest just before flowering. Non-toxic to pets. Harvest regularly to promote bushy growth. Pinch off flower buds to extend leaf production.
Acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.5). Partial shade in hot climates. Avoid hard frost. Harvest young leaves (two leaves and a bud). Prune to encourage bush growth.

Water when soil is dry (every 1-2 weeks once established). Well-drained soil essential. Drought tolerant once established. Full sun preferred (6-8 hours daily). Fertilize sparingly in spring. Harvest regularly by cutting stems. Can be grown as groundcover or in containers. Perennial - may need protection in very cold climates. Reduce watering in winter when growth slows. Remove yellowing or damaged leaves promptly.

Keep soil evenly moist but not waterlogged. Well-drained, rich soil preferred. Partial shade preferred. Fertilize monthly with balanced fertilizer. Plant rhizome pieces. Harvest when leaves die back (8-10 months). Can be grown in containers. Related to ginger. Popular spice and natural dye. Requires warm climate - protect from frost. Reduce watering in winter when growth slows. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Water frequently and abundantly - Vietnamese coriander is a semi-aquatic plant that thrives in consistently wet to boggy conditions and will wilt rapidly if allowed to dry out. Partial shade to full shade (3-5 hours of sun daily); unlike most herbs, it prefers shade and its leaves scorch in intense direct sun. Fertilize every 2-3 weeks with a balanced liquid fertilizer during the growing season. An excellent cilantro substitute in hot climates since it does not bolt in heat. Propagates effortlessly from stem cuttings placed in water. Grows as a spreading ground cover in tropical areas; in temperate zones, bring containers indoors before frost as it is not frost hardy. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Keep soil consistently moist — grows naturally along mountain stream beds. Cool shade essential; cannot tolerate heat above 20°C or direct sun. Very high humidity required. Extremely slow growing — takes 18-24 months to produce a usable rhizome. Non-toxic. Harvest regularly to promote bushy growth. Pinch off flower buds to extend leaf production.

Full sun. Well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil. Drought tolerant once established. Harvest hay at 10% bloom. Inoculate seed with rhizobia. Remove flower stems and any damaged or rotting leaves promptly.
Full sun. Well-drained soil. Warm-season crop. Harvest when seed heads dry and seeds rattle. Thresh when fully dry. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.
Full sun. Well-drained soil. Cool-season crop. Harvest when heads bend and kernels hard. Two-row and six-row varieties. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged — high water needs in tropical conditions. Partial shade to filtered sun; protect from intense afternoon sun. Rich, acidic, well-drained soil with high organic matter. Fertilize every 2-3 months with balanced fertilizer. Needs a support structure to climb (grows 4-5m). Very high humidity (80%+) essential. Harvest green for green peppercorns, let dry on vine for black pepper, or soak and remove skin for white pepper. Minimum temperature 20°C. Non-toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Full sun. Any well-drained soil. Sow late spring to midsummer. Harvest when most seeds brown (lower seeds may shatter). Good green manure. Minimal pruning needed. Remove damaged or diseased plant material.

Keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged; sensitive to both drought and standing water. Partial shade preferred—naturally an understory tree. Very high humidity (80%+) essential. Rich, well-draining acidic soil (pH 5.0-6.5). Fertilize monthly with balanced fertilizer during growing season. Flowers and fruits grow directly from the trunk (cauliflory). Needs temperatures above 18°C year-round. Theobromine in all parts is toxic to pets. Minimal pruning needed. Remove damaged or diseased plant material.

Sow in early spring or fall depending on variety (spring or winter type). Full sun required. Water regularly during flowering for best seed set. Harvest when pods turn brown and seeds rattle. Prefers well-drained, fertile soil. Winter varieties need cold period for vernalization. Self-pollinating but benefits from bee activity. Non-toxic. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Plant stem cuttings in well-drained soil after last frost. Full sun required. Water regularly during establishment, then drought-tolerant once established. Harvest roots 8-12 months after planting. Must be properly processed (soaked, fermented, or cooked) before eating to remove cyanogenic compounds. Prefers sandy loam. All raw parts toxic — must be processed before consumption. Toxic to pets. Minimal pruning needed. Remove damaged or diseased plant material.
Full sun. Well-drained, neutral soil. Inoculate with rhizobia. Harvest when pods dry and rattle. Allow plants to dry before threshing. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Water regularly to keep soil consistently moist; reduce slightly in cooler months. Partial shade to full sun — young trees prefer some protection from intense sun. Rich, acidic, well-drained sandy loam. Fertilize every 2-3 months. Bark is harvested by coppicing — cut stems at ground level during the rainy season; new shoots produce the best bark. First harvest after 2-3 years. Ceylon cinnamon has a more delicate flavor than cassia. Can be grown as a houseplant in cooler climates (aromatic leaves). Mildly toxic to pets in large quantities. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Water regularly — needs consistent moisture year-round in tropical conditions. Partial shade when young; full sun once established. Rich, acidic, well-drained volcanic or loamy soil. Fertilize 2-3 times per year with organic fertilizer. Harvest flower buds when they turn pink but before they open — timing is critical for quality. First harvest after 5-7 years. Very slow-growing but extremely long-lived. Thrives near the coast in equatorial climates. Eugenol in cloves is toxic to cats and dogs — toxic to pets. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.
Full sun to partial shade. Well-drained soil. Inoculate seed. Harvest hay at early bloom. Good for rotation and soil building. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Water occasionally — quite drought tolerant once established. Full sun to partial shade. Adapts to most soil types. Self-seeding and spreading. Tolerates mowing and foot traffic. Often used as a lawn alternative or companion plant. Non-toxic. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Keep soil evenly moist but not soggy; water when top 2 cm dries. Bright indirect light—scorches in direct sun. High humidity (60%+) preferred; mist regularly. Rich, well-draining, acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5). Fertilize every 2 weeks spring through summer with balanced acidic fertilizer. May produce fragrant white flowers and red berries indoors after 3-5 years. Prefers cool nights (15-18°C). All parts except the beans are toxic to pets (caffeine). Minimal pruning needed. Remove damaged or diseased plant material.
Full sun. Rich, well-drained soil. Plant after soil warms. Heavy feeder—nitrogen critical. Harvest when husks dry and kernels hard (dent stage). Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.
Full sun. Well-drained soil. Warm-season crop. Harvest when bolls open and lint fluffs. Defoliate before pick for cleaner harvest. Remove flower stems and any damaged or rotting leaves promptly.
Full sun. Well-drained soil. Warm-season. Harvest dry beans when pods brown and rattle. Bush and vining types available. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Full sun. Cool-season—plant early spring or fall. Inoculate with rhizobia. Harvest green pods when plump or dry beans when pods brown. Minimal pruning needed. Remove damaged or diseased plant material.
Full sun. Well-drained soil. Plant early spring. Harvest when seed capsules brown (90–110 days). Fiber types pulled when flowering. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Keep soil consistently moist during seedling stage; once established, moderate watering every 3-5 days. Full sun essential—at least 6 hours daily for optimal growth. Medium humidity fine. Deep, well-draining, nutrient-rich soil (pH 6.0-7.0). Heavy nitrogen feeder during vegetative growth; switch to phosphorus-potassium at flowering. Plant after last frost when soil reaches 10°C. Grows very fast—3-4 meters in one season. Non-toxic (industrial hemp contains negligible THC). Minimal pruning needed. Remove damaged or diseased plant material.

Full sun. Well-drained soil. Provide tall support (15–20 ft). Toxic to dogs—causes dangerous fever. Harvest cones when papery and aromatic (late summer). Toxic to pets. Remove dead, rotten, diseased leaves and the parts that may affect the good appearance

Water abundantly — jute requires high moisture and thrives in floodplain soils. Full sun essential. Rich, alluvial, moisture-retentive soil. Warm, humid tropical climate required (minimum 20°C). Grows extremely fast (3-4m in 4 months). Harvest when plants flower; stems are retted (soaked) in water for 2-3 weeks to extract fiber. Bangladesh and India produce over 90% of world supply. Leaves of C. olitorius are edible and popular in Middle Eastern and African cuisine (molokhia). Non-toxic to pets. Minimal pruning needed. Remove damaged or diseased plant material.
Full sun. Well-drained soil. Cool-season crop. Harvest when pods dry and seeds rattle. Low-growing; combine or hand harvest. Minimal pruning needed. Remove damaged or diseased plant material.
Full sun. Well-drained soil. Warm-season. Harvest when seed heads dry. Birds love it—harvest promptly when ripe. Minimal pruning needed. Remove damaged or diseased plant material.
Full sun. Well-drained soil. Warm-season. Harvest dry beans when pods turn dark and rattle. Also grown for sprouts. Remove flower stems and any damaged or rotting leaves promptly.
Full sun. Well-drained soil. Cool-season. Harvest when pods dry and seeds rattle. Can be used as cover crop or green manure. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Water regularly to maintain consistent moisture; reduce slightly during cooler dry season. Partial shade to filtered light — protect from direct afternoon sun. Deep, rich, acidic, well-drained volcanic soil. Fertilize 2-3 times per year with organic fertilizer high in potassium. Dioecious — plant both male and female trees; ratio of 1 male per 10 females. First harvest after 7-9 years. Fruits split when ripe to reveal the bright red mace covering the seed. Toxic in large doses to humans (contains myristicin); toxic to pets. Minimal pruning needed. Remove damaged or diseased plant material.

Full sun. Tolerates heavy, moist soil. Cool-season crop. Harvest when panicles golden and kernels in hard-dough stage. Good nurse crop. Minimal pruning needed. Remove damaged or diseased plant material.

Water regularly — needs consistent moisture and high rainfall (1800-2500mm/year). Full sun essential. Well-drained, deep, loamy soil. Fertilize heavily and regularly (4-6 times per year) with balanced fertilizer high in potassium. Begins fruiting at 3-4 years; peak production at 8-15 years. Produces fruit bunches year-round in equatorial climates. A single tree can yield 3-4 tonnes of fruit per year. Highly controversial due to deforestation concerns — sustainable certification (RSPO) encouraged. Non-toxic to pets. Minimal pruning needed. Remove damaged or diseased plant material.
Full sun. Light, sandy, well-drained soil. Warm-season. Harvest when foliage yellows; dig before frost. Cure 2–3 weeks before storage. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Drought-tolerant once established; water moderately during flowering and pod development. Full sun essential—at least 6 hours daily. Medium humidity fine. Tolerates poor soils—as a legume, it fixes nitrogen and actually improves soil fertility. Minimal fertilizer needed; too much nitrogen promotes leaves over pods. Can grow as an annual or short-lived perennial in frost-free areas. Pods can be harvested green or dry. Excellent intercrop companion. Non-toxic to humans and animals. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.
Full sun. Well-drained soil. Cool-season; frost tolerant. Harvest when seed heads dry and seeds rattle. Rinse before cooking. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.
Full sun. Lowland rice needs flooded fields or constant moisture. Upland rice tolerates drier conditions. Harvest when panicles golden and grains hard. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Water regularly — needs high, consistent rainfall (2000+mm/year). Full sun essential. Deep, acidic, well-drained laterite or loamy soil. Fertilize 3-4 times per year. Latex tapping begins at 5-7 years: a diagonal cut in the bark allows milky latex to flow into a collection cup. Trees can be tapped for 25-30 years. Native to the Amazon; now primarily grown in Southeast Asia (Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia produce 70% of world supply). Latex sap can cause skin irritation. Mildly toxic to pets. Remove yellowing or damaged leaves promptly.
Full sun. Tolerates poor, acidic soil. Winter rye planted fall. Harvest when heads golden. Excellent cover crop for biomass. Minimal pruning needed. Remove damaged or diseased plant material.
Full sun. Well-drained soil. Drought tolerant. Harvest when plants dry and seeds loosen. Oil and confection types available. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Full sun. Warm, well-drained soil. Warm-season. Harvest when lower capsules brown—plants mature unevenly. Non-shattering varieties available. Minimal pruning needed. Remove damaged or diseased plant material.

Water sparingly — extremely drought tolerant once established. Full sun essential. Well-drained, even rocky or sandy soil. Minimal fertilization needed. Leaves are cut from the outer rosette starting at 2-3 years and can be harvested every 6-12 months. Plant dies after flowering (monocarpic) at 7-12 years, producing a tall flower spike up to 6m. Produces bulbils and suckers for propagation. Major production in Brazil, Tanzania, and Kenya. Leaf edges have sharp spines. Mildly toxic to pets (saponins). Minimal pruning needed. Remove damaged or diseased plant material.
Full sun. Well-drained soil. Warm-season. Harvest grain when heads hard and red; syrup when stalks sweet. Frost-sensitive. Remove flower stems and any damaged or rotting leaves promptly.
Full sun. Well-drained soil. Warm-season. Harvest when pods dry and beans rattle. Inoculate with rhizobia. Rotate with corn. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Direct sow seeds 2cm deep after last frost, spacing 15cm apart. Full sun required. Keep soil consistently moist during root development. Harvest after 90-100 days when roots are 7-10cm diameter. Prefers loose, well-drained soil free of rocks. Fertilize at planting with balanced fertilizer. Cool-season crop; best in spring or fall. Non-toxic. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.
Full sun. Tropical—frost kills. Plant stem cuttings (setts). Harvest when canes mature (12–24 months). Needs abundant water and heat. Remove flower stems and any damaged or rotting leaves promptly.
Full sun. Well-drained soil. Warm-season. Harvest when back of heads yellow and seeds dry. Protect from birds with bags or netting. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.
Full sun. Light, sandy soil. Warm-season. Plant slips. Harvest before frost when roots reach size. Cure 1–2 weeks for storage. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.
Full sun. Well-drained soil. Warm-season. Harvest when seed heads dry. Cut and cure in field; thresh carefully—seeds easily lost. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.
Full sun. Well-drained soil. Water regularly. Toxic to pets—nicotine in all plant parts. Keep away from animals and children. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Full sun. Well-drained soil. Winter wheat planted fall; spring wheat in spring. Harvest when heads golden and kernels hard (combine or cut when dry). Remove flower stems and any damaged or rotting leaves promptly.

Water regularly to keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged. Partial shade to filtered sun — grows naturally in the understory. Acidic, well-drained, red laterite soil rich in iron. Fertilize 2-3 times per year. Harvest by pruning branches — the plant regrows vigorously. First harvest after 3-4 years. Leaves are dried and often smoked to produce the traditional mate tea, traditionally consumed from a gourd (mate) with a metal straw (bombilla). Contains caffeine, theobromine, and many antioxidants. Non-toxic to pets.

Soak seeds 8-12 hours. Rinse 2-3× daily; drain thoroughly. No light needed during sprouting. Harvest in 3-5 days when tails are 1-2 inches. Sweet, nutty flavor. No fertilizer needed. Rich in protein, fiber, and folate. Remove flower stems and any damaged or rotting leaves promptly.

Soak seeds 4-8 hours. Rinse 2× daily; drain well. Keep in dark first 3 days, then move to indirect light for greening. Harvest in 5-7 days. Mild, nutty flavor. No fertilizer. Rich in vitamins K and C. Store refrigerated up to 5 days. Remove flower stems and any damaged or rotting leaves promptly.

Sow on moist medium; mist to keep damp. Do not cover seeds (need light to germinate). Bright indirect light once sprouted. Mist 1-2× daily. Harvest in 8-12 days. Vibrant magenta stems with mild, earthy flavor. Rich in protein and lysine. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Sow on moist medium; press gently. Mist 1-2× daily. Bright indirect light. Harvest in 7-10 days at first true leaves. Spicy, peppery flavor—milder than mature arugula. No fertilizer. Fast growing; great for beginners. Rich in vitamins A and K. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Soak seeds 2-4 hours (mucilaginous coating). Sow on moist medium. Mist 1-2× daily. Bright indirect light Harvest in 10-16 days. Concentrated basil aroma. Slow germinator—be patient. Rich in polyphenols. Remove yellowing or damaged leaves promptly.

Soak seed clusters 8-12 hours. Sow on moist medium, press in. Mist 1-2× daily. Bright indirect light. Harvest in 10-14 days. Stunning ruby-red stems with earthy, sweet flavor. Each 'seed' produces multiple sprouts. Rich in iron and betalains. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Sow on moist medium; mist to keep damp. Bright indirect light. Harvest in 7-10 days at cotyledon stage. Slightly spicy, broccoli-like flavor with a hint of mustard. No fertilizer. Rich in sulforaphane and vitamins A and C. Harvest by cutting at soil level when cotyledons or first true leaves appear.

Soak seeds 6-8 hours. Rinse 2× daily; drain thoroughly. Keep dark first 3 days, then bright indirect light. Harvest in 5-7 days. Mild, slightly spicy. One of the richest food sources of sulforaphane—a potent antioxidant. Store refrigerated. Harvest by cutting at soil level when cotyledons or first true leaves appear.

Soak seeds 15-30 minutes only (over-soaking causes mushiness). Rinse 2× daily; drain very well. Bright indirect light for greening. Harvest in 7-10 days. Mild, lettuce-like flavor. Remove hulls before eating. Rich in rutin and complete protein. Harvest by cutting at soil level when cotyledons or first true leaves appear.

Sow on moist medium; press in. Keep moist—mist 2× daily. Bright indirect light. Slow germinator; harvest in 14-18 days. Concentrated carrot flavor; wispy, feathery tops. Patience required—one of the slower microgreens. Rich in beta-carotene. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Gently crush seed husks before soaking 8-12 hours. Sow on moist medium. Mist 1-2× daily. Bright indirect light. Harvest in 14-21 days. Full cilantro aroma; slow germinator. Each husk produces 2 plants. Rich in vitamins A and K. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Soak seeds 4-8 hours. Rinse 2× daily; drain well. Keep dark first 3 days, then move to indirect light. Harvest in 5-7 days. Mild, fresh, slightly sweet flavor. Tiny and delicate. No fertilizer. Rich in isoflavones and vitamins A and C. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Sow on moist paper towel or medium; seeds stick when wet (mucilaginous). Mist 1-2× daily—do not rinse. Bright indirect light. Harvest in 5-7 days. Peppery, tangy flavor. One of the fastest and easiest microgreens. Rich in vitamins A, C, and K. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Sow on moist medium; press gently. Mist 1-2× daily. Bright indirect light. Harvest in 14-21 days at cotyledon stage. Concentrated dill flavor—excellent with fish and eggs. Slow germinator; requires patience. Rich in antioxidants. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Soak seeds 8-12 hours. Rinse 2× daily; drain well. Keep dark. Harvest in 3-5 days. Slightly bitter, maple-like flavor; popular in Indian cuisine. Quick and easy to grow. Rich in iron, protein, and soluble fiber. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Sow on moist medium; press gently. Mist 1-2× daily. Bright indirect light. Harvest in 8-12 days. Mild, slightly sweet—less bitter than mature kale. Purple or green varieties. No fertilizer. Rich in vitamins A, C, K, and calcium. Harvest by cutting at soil level when cotyledons or first true leaves appear.

Soak seeds 8-12 hours. Sow on moist medium; keep damp. Mist 1-2× daily. Bright indirect light. Harvest in 12-14 days. Delicate onion-leek flavor, milder than mature leeks. Thin, elegant garnish. Rich in folate and vitamin K. Remove dead or damaged foliage promptly.

Soak seeds 8-12 hours. Rinse 2-3× daily; drain thoroughly. Keep dark. Harvest in 3-5 days when tails are 1/2-1 inch. Mild, slightly sweet, earthy. Best cooked lightly or added to stir-fries.
